question.text: After a bonus issue, what happens to the total value of a shareholder's holdings (immediately, before any market movement)?

answer.text: It remains the same as the share price adjusts proportionally downward
It decreases because new shares dilute the value
It increases by the bonus ratio
It increases because bonus shares are issued from free reserves

explanation.text: The Logic: A bonus issue distributes additional shares to existing shareholders out of the company's free reserves, without any cash contribution from the shareholders, and increases the total number of outstanding shares. Because no new economic value flows into the company, its market capitalisation immediately after the bonus is essentially unchanged, and the share price adjusts downward proportionally to reflect the larger share count. As a result, the total value of a shareholder's holdings immediately after the bonus (before any market movement) remains broadly the same — for example, 100 shares at Rs.200 each (Rs.20,000) becoming 200 shares at approximately Rs.100 each (still around Rs.20,000) after a 1:1 bonus. The Trap: Treating the bonus as dilutive in value to existing shareholders confuses share-count dilution with economic dilution; existing shareholders receive the new shares pro-rata so their proportionate ownership is preserved. Treating the bonus as a value increase by the bonus ratio ignores the proportional price adjustment. Treating the issuance from free reserves as an immediate value gain confuses the accounting source of the bonus with its market-value impact, which is broadly neutral immediately after the action. Note: The cited workbook chapter supports the description of a bonus issue as an issuance of additional shares without shareholder capital contribution that increases outstanding shares; the workbook's discussion of "unchanged value due to proportional price adjustment" appears in the context of stock splits/consolidations rather than the bonus-issue section. The framing above is general industry/market-mechanics knowledge applied to a bonus issue rather than a direct workbook citation.
